newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Call for review of South African budget rollovers.
newsitem.headline: Call for review of South African budget rollovers.

text.p: The South African government needed to address the issue of rollovers as they represented a threat to its overall management of the economy, economists said this week.

South Africa's financial markets were buoyed earlier this week by reports that the possible cancellation of some five billion rand of an estimated 12.5 billion rand in rollovers would help government reduce its budget deficit -- projected at 5.1 percent in fiscal 1996/97.
The bond market, in particular, rallied on the news, with the key R150 stock breaking below the key 16.00 percent yield on Tuesday.

But Equisec economist Dawie Roodt said the market was wrong to see rollovers as "money in the kitty", since they were in fact amounts approved in a previous fiscal year which had neither been spent nor funded.
The hefty rollovers have accumulated largely as a result of adminstrative backlogs in delivery of reconstruction and development projects, analysts said.
"What has actually happened in the last few years is that rollovers have accumulated while the total budgeted expenditure was spent," Roodt said.
"If the rollovers were actually spent, the deficit would have been higher," he added.
Roodt said the "cutting" of rollovers did not imply government expenditure would be reduced.
"Government finance is a dynamic process and projects and programmes are approved and cut on a continuous basis. A cut somewhere usually means additional spending somewhere else."
Edward Osborn, strategic economist at Edey Rogers and Co, said that while rollovers held no implications for the deficit, they were an issue that government needed to address.
"There is a very sizeable amount of these rollovers which are not funds as such...They are simply authorisations to spend," he said.

"They represent a very serious problem for government because there is this tremendous overhang of past authorisations and that means that there could be the need for additional funding from the market," Osborn said.
"It is that threat, which is very considerable, which makes this whole business of rollovers a very important issue that has to be properly addressed."
Economists said some light could be shed on the actual amount of rollovers when government's adjustment budget was presented on February 13.
However, a Finance Department official said final clarity on the issue was only likely to emerge when its books were closed at the end of July.
Government's gross borrowing requirement for fiscal 1996/97 is 45.105 billion rand, of which it had financed 33.33 billion rand by the end of December 1996.
